title: Tax reforms 'to change house prices forever'
full_text:
A sharp downturn in housing market sentiment caused by the Albanese government's tax changes has forced economists to downgrade forecasts and shave a permanent 5 per cent off house prices, even as Jim Chalmers insists Treasury modelling puts the effects of Labor's budget measures at just a 2 per cent reduction in growth.
The treasurer admitted on Thursday that the government's changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing announced in the federal budget were "one of a number of reasons" behind the intensifying house price falls across the country.
"I think that there's not one factor driving softness in the housing market," he told the ABC. "We saw house prices and auction clearance rates soften even before the budget, reacting to interest rate changes and developments in the economy more broadly."
Chalmers also maintained the adjustment in house prices was "not unusual", saying historically on "at least seven different occasions, we've seen house prices come off, and that's because they react to things like interest rate movements, like developments in the global and domestic economy".
The property downturn was interrogated during a Senate committee on intergenerational housing inequity in Canberra on Thursday that included testimony by economists from major banks and Reserve Bank chief economist Sarah Hunter.
Hunter refused to be drawn by Liberal senator Andrew Bragg on the Treasury's projections that the tax changes would lead to 35,000 fewer dwellings or the specific role of the changes in the housing downturn.
"The tax changes have come together with a number of other factors that have caused house prices to decline across most parts of the country now," Hunter said.
She acknowledged that the bank was concerned about rental prices, which were growing faster than before the pandemic.
"We're generally trying to bring inflation down, and a part of that is slower rental growth," she said.
Some major banks revised their forecasts this week, pointing to a deeper decline in the property market. Commonwealth Bank and Goldman Sachs economists have tipped dwelling prices to fall about 9 per cent from peak to trough, while HSBC has predicted a 13 per cent decline.
"Our estimate at the time of the budget was that the changes would shave around 5 per cent off the level of prices over the long term, and we haven't changed that," CBA senior economist Trent Saunders said.
The bank's updated forecasts stemmed from an unexpected major shift in housing market sentiment prompted by the Albanese government's tax reforms, which threatens to deepen the short-term slump and push any recovery in house prices beyond CBA's forecasting horizon.
Goldman Sachs chief economist for Australia Andrew Boak said it was possible further adverse reaction from investors to the tax changes could force another downward revision in the bank's dwelling price forecasts.
Boak's analysis shows the downturn is already set to be "historically large", hitting a lower trough than any downturn since 1982, but he said, "the key thing is whether this adjustment in the housing market continues in an orderly way".
"So far it's been, as far as I can see, quite an orderly adjustment," he said.
"The scenarios that you're really worried about [are when] a housing cycle becomes a debt deleveraging cycle, where people are defaulting because they lose their jobs, huge chunks of the mortgagor cohort are in negative equity - I think those risks are actually relatively low and manageable. We're definitely looking at a period of weaker growth, but I think a manageable unwind."
